summary: Adds a BURL command to mail submission so a client can tell the submission server to fetch message content from an IMAP server. The client can send mail built from stored content without downloading it and uploading it again. It is a proposed standard.

eli5.summary: Instead of carrying a package to the post office, you tell the post office to pick it up from the warehouse where it already is.

subtitle: A BURL command that lets a mail submission server pull a message from an IMAP server instead of making the client upload it.

tldr.problem: A mail client that already has message content stored on an IMAP server would normally have to download it and upload it again to send it.
tldr.mechanism: The BURL command replaces DATA in message submission. The client gives an IMAP URL, and the submission server fetches the content from the IMAP server and includes it in the message.
tldr.outcome: A client on a slow link can forward stored content without moving it through itself. The RFC also warns that this makes abuse easier, so servers need authentication, logging and rate limits. It is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 3463.

today: RFC 4468 is a Proposed Standard. It has been updated by RFC 5248, and it updates RFC 3463 by adding two enhanced status codes.

sections.title: Why Fetch Content at Submission Time
sections.content:
RFC 4468 extends the standard Message Submission protocol (RFC 4409) so that data can be fetched from an IMAP server at the moment a message is submitted. The new command is BURL.

It may be used together with the CHUNKING mechanism (RFC 3030), so that some chunks of a message come from an external IMAP server. The result is the ability to forward an email message without first downloading it to the client.
sections.eli5: You normally have to fetch your toy from the shelf and hand it over. Here you just point at the shelf and the other person grabs it.

sections.title: Advertising the BURL Extension
sections.content:
The extension is named BURL, and the EHLO keyword is also BURL. It extends the Message Submission protocol on port 587. It MUST NOT be advertised by a regular SMTP server on port 25 that acts as a relay for incoming mail from other SMTP relays.

The keyword can carry arguments. The only one defined is imap, which MUST be present to use IMAP URLs with BURL. Clients MUST ignore other arguments unless a later IETF standards track specification defines them.

Arguments may change after SMTP AUTH. A server that advertises BURL with no arguments before authentication is saying that BURL is supported but authentication is required to use it.
sections.eli5: The server holds up a sign saying which special tricks it knows. Some tricks only show up on the sign after you prove who you are.

sections.title: The BURL Transaction
sections.content:
BURL is used in place of DATA, and only after at least one successful RCPT TO. A simple transaction is MAIL FROM, one or more RCPT TO, and a BURL command with the LAST tag. The command carries an IMAP URL that points to a fully formed message ready for injection into the SMTP infrastructure.

If no valid recipient was given, BURL fails and the URL is never resolved. If at least one recipient is valid, the server resolves the URL before it answers the command. If the fetch fails, the server fails the whole transaction.

If the server also advertises PIPELINING, the client may send the whole transaction in one round trip. If it advertises CHUNKING as well, BURL and BDAT commands may be interleaved until one of them ends the transaction with LAST. The client MUST wait for the result of the LAST command before starting a new transaction.
sections.eli5: You tell the post office who the letter is for, then say where the letter is sitting. They go and get it before telling you yes. If they cannot find it, the whole delivery is cancelled.

sections.title: How the Submission Server Reaches IMAP
sections.content:
When imap is advertised, the server supports the URLAUTH form of IMAP URLs (RFC 4467) and has the credentials to resolve urlauth=submit+ URLs for its own domain. The server uses its own configurable submit credentials; the string submit is suggested as the default authentication identity, with no default password. If the URL uses the submit+ prefix, the server MUST refuse the command unless the userid in the URL matches the client's authorization identity.

After SMTP AUTH, the server may instead advertise a prearranged trust relationship with one IMAP server, as an argument like imap://imap.example.com. Then it accepts regular IMAP URLs on that server that the authenticated user can access. This form does not imply URLAUTH support; a server must advertise both forms to support both. A regular URL is fetched using the client's authorization identity.

The submission server acts as an IMAP client, so it is subject to the mandatory-to-implement capabilities and security considerations of RFC 3501. In practice it needs a configuration that uses STARTTLS followed by SASL PLAIN. It SHOULD forward the client's credentials only if it knows the IMAP server is in the same administrative domain.
sections.eli5: The post office needs permission to open your warehouse. Either you hand over a special one-time pass, or the post office and the warehouse already trust each other.

sections.title: 8-Bit and Binary Content
sections.content:
A submission server that advertises BURL MUST also advertise 8BITMIME and perform the down conversion that RFC 1652 describes if 8-bit data arrives via BURL and is passed to a 7-bit server. If the URL refers to binary data, the server MAY refuse the command or down convert as Binary SMTP (RFC 3030) describes.

The server MAY also refuse a BURL or BURL and BDAT combination that results in un-encoded 8-bit data in mail or MIME headers. Alternatively it may accept the data and down convert to MIME header encoding.
sections.eli5: Some mail trucks only carry plain letters. If your package has fancy contents, the post office either repacks it into a plain form or says no.

sections.title: Enhanced Status Codes and Replies
sections.content:
Servers that advertise ENHANCEDSTATUSCODES use the codes of RFC 3463. BURL adds two new ones: X.6.6 (message content not available, because it could not be fetched from a remote system) and X.7.8 (trust relationship required, because the server needs a configured trust relationship with a third-party server to reach the content). That is how this RFC updates RFC 3463.

The RFC lists example replies to BURL. The list is not exhaustive, and clients MUST tolerate any valid SMTP response code. A success without LAST returns 250 2.5.0 while waiting for more BURL or BDAT commands, but the content is not necessarily committed to persistent storage yet.
sections.eli5: When something goes wrong, the post office gives you a numbered slip saying why, such as the warehouse being closed or not trusted.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Implementations should fetch the URL content before applying content-based defenses such as virus filtering, size limits and spam filtering, so those still work. BURL also makes abuse easier: a device on a slow link, such as a programmable cell phone, could become a significant source of bulk email or viruses. The RFC suggests mandatory authentication, logging that ties unique client identifiers to transactions, limits on reuse of the same IMAP URL, rate limits, recipient count limits and content filters.

URLAUTH URLs sent in the clear can expose the authorization token to eavesdroppers, so STARTTLS on both SMTP and IMAP, required by configuration, is recommended. Trust relationships that use super-user proxy credentials are strongly discouraged, because a compromised submission server should not expose every IMAP account.

A user could also point the server at an IMAP server under their control. The server's IMAP client code must therefore cope with arbitrary input sizes (including large IMAP literals) and arbitrary delays, and a server that only uses submit credentials with a fixed set of trusted IMAP servers avoids leaking them.
sections.eli5: A pass that lets the post office fetch things can also be misused, so the post office has to check who is asking, keep a log, and not hand its keys to strangers.
